transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-10-01 09:30 PT
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Rohit Patel (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Redwood CSM), David Kim (Aurora Sr. ML Eng), Priya Shah (Aurora Platform), Marcus Lee (Aurora Head of AI), Sofia Ramos (Aurora Security)

Summary:
Quick POC weekly sync focused on prefix/KV cache warmup behavior, session reuse heuristics, and calibration of eviction thresholds. Reviewed latest KV-hitrate dashboard (24h snapshot), discussed noise from multi-session churn, clarified security/KMS concerns for Private deploy, and agreed next steps: longer stress test, prompt-set export, and infra feasibility discussion.

Topics covered:
- KV cache hit rate trends and anomalies
- Prefix similarity vs prompt normalization
- Session warmup / session affinity tradeoffs
- Eviction thresholds and cost/latency SLOs
- Private deployment & KMS implications

Action items (captured inline as well): see metadata above

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Chen (Redwood): Okay let's kick off, hey everyone, thanks for joining. Uh quick roll call — we good?
[00:18] David Kim (Aurora): Yep, here. Sorry was pulling up the dashboard, bit of wifi blip earlier.
[00:28] Rohit Patel (Redwood): No worries. I'll start with the KV-hitrate snapshot we ran overnight. Quick note: this was with the relaxed prefix match set to 0.7 and eviction to 75%.
[00:45] Priya Shah (Aurora): Can you remind us what 0.7 means in practice? We've had some mismatches before.
[01:02] Rohit Patel (Redwood): Yeah, so uh 0.7 is cosine threshold on the prefix embedding similarity — basically prompts that share 70% similarity are considered cacheable for prefix reuse. We observed about a 28% hit rate across the 24h window.
[01:25] Marcus Lee (Aurora): 28% seems low compared to your earlier demo numbers. Is that because of session churn?
[01:38] Rohit Patel (Redwood): Partly. We see a lot of short sessions — like single-turn chats — which don't warm the KV cache. Also you have a high variance in prompt canonicalization, so superficially different prompts with the same intent aren't matching.
[01:58] Maya Chen (Redwood): To add, the demo numbers were from a sanitized workload with batched prefixes; production is messier.
[02:10] David Kim (Aurora): Got it. We do have lots of micro-interactions. Is there a way to hold session affinity longer without blowing up memory?
[02:25] Rohit Patel (Redwood): Yes that's the calibration tradeoff. You can increase session TTL or tune the eviction policy to favor recently active sessions, but cost rises. For example, lowering eviction threshold from 75% to 60% improved hit rate to ~35% in one trial, but memory footprint grew ~18%.
[02:50] Sofia Ramos (Aurora, Security): Any impact on data residency / logs if we warm sessions across regions? We need to map that to our compliance policy.
[03:03] Lena Ortiz (Redwood CSM): Good flag. If you choose cross-region warmup, we'll surface the trace and can enforce region pinning; for Private deploy we'd align with your VPC/KMS controls.
[03:20] Priya Shah (Aurora): We'd prefer VPC-bound caching for PHI-sensitive workloads. Is Redwood's private option mature for that?
[03:34] Maya Chen (Redwood): Yes, Private supports VPC + customer KMS. We'll need to verify HSM requirements if you have an HSM-backed KMS — that's something Sofia's team flagged earlier.
[03:48] David Kim (Aurora): Back to the hit rate, Rohit, you mentioned normalization. What pre-processing are you doing by default?
[03:58] Rohit Patel (Redwood): We do light token normalization, whitespace collapse, and lowercasing; we do NOT strip domain-specific stopwords by default. For your workload, adding a prompt canonicalizer (strip session ids, timestamps, and common template tokens) could bump similarity a lot.
[04:18] Marcus Lee (Aurora): That could help — we have a lot of telemetry tokens in prompts.
[04:26] Rohit Patel (Redwood): If you can provide 1k representative prompts, we can run a quick experiment and report back.
[04:34] David Kim (Aurora): We'll get that to you.
[04:38] Maya Chen (Redwood): Great. Now let's step through the dashboard screenshots Rohit dropped in the chat. Rohit, can you narrate the anomalous dip around 03:00 UTC?
[04:50] Rohit Patel (Redwood): Sure, so around 03:00 we saw a sudden drop from 32% to 18% hit rate—looking at request logs it's a burst of one-off queries from a new mobile client version that sends verbose metadata in the prompt. So again, canonicalization would catch that.
[05:12] Priya Shah (Aurora): That was our mobile v2 rollout — good catch. We'll add a client-side header to avoid plopping metadata into the prompt.
[05:23] David Kim (Aurora): On eviction, what's the recommendation for TTL for interactive flows vs async batch jobs?
[05:33] Rohit Patel (Redwood): Interactive flows usually do well with shorter TTL but sticky session affinity — say 15-30 minutes — to keep working set small. For async batch jobs, you can be more aggressive on reuse because queries are more uniform; there TTLs can be 1-2 hours depending on memory.
[05:56] Marcus Lee (Aurora): If we increase prefix matching threshold to 0.8 does that reduce false positives?
[06:04] Rohit Patel (Redwood): Yes higher threshold is stricter — you'll see fewer mismatches, lower quality regressions, but lower hit rate. It's another tradeoff between latency/cost and output quality.
[06:20] Sofia Ramos (Aurora): From security side, we need to ensure cache entries are encrypted at rest and keys are not accessible to Redwood operators — is that possible in Private?
[06:33] Maya Chen (Redwood): In Private, with customer-managed KMS, you retain key control. We can also enable audit logs that tie key usage to your principal. We'll share the architecture doc after this call.
[06:48] Priya Shah (Aurora): Awesome — please add HSM note if applicable.
[06:54] Rohit Patel (Redwood): Will do. Moving on, we tried a hybrid prefetch heuristic yesterday: prefetch top 5 predicted continuations for recurring prompts and pinned them into the KV. Hit rate jumped briefly but then we saw eviction churn because the prefetch population didn't align with live traffic.
[07:16] David Kim (Aurora): So prefetch can help but must be tuned to your traffic distribution. Any way to make prefetch adaptive?
[07:25] Rohit Patel (Redwood): Yes — adaptive prefetch: weigh candidates by recent frequency + session recency. We'll prototype a version that decays prefetch weight over time.
[07:37] Marcus Lee (Aurora): How invasive is that to our integration?
[07:42] Rohit Patel (Redwood): Minimal — it's a server-side policy. You can toggle it on/off per route.
[07:50] Maya Chen (Redwood): Quick check — what's acceptable latency bump for prefetch misfires?
[07:58] Rohit Patel (Redwood): In our tests misfires cost around 5-12ms on average per request because of extra KV checks; biggest cost is memory.
[08:10] Priya Shah (Aurora): Memory is our main cap right now; we have a 64GB pool per node. Any rule-of-thumb for nodes required?
[08:20] Rohit Patel (Redwood): With your current workload and TTL of 30m and 60% eviction, we'd estimate 3-4 nodes for headroom. If you move eviction to 75% you might drop to 2-3 nodes. We'll include an updated sizing calc in the follow-up.
[08:37] David Kim (Aurora): Can Redwood expose per-prefix cost breakdown? Ops asked for token-cost alignment to billing.
[08:45] Lena Ortiz (Redwood CSM): Yes the console has token-level breakdown per route + model; for per-prefix cost we can add a small instrumentation job that attributes KV hits to prefix families. We'll propose a wireframe.
[09:00] Marcus Lee (Aurora): About the canonicalizer — is that something we run client-side or you recommend a Redwood-side pipeline?
[09:09] Rohit Patel (Redwood): Either works. Client-side reduces sending PII and saves token cost; Redwood-side gives you centralized controls and faster iteration. For sensitive PHI workloads, we usually recommend client-side canonicalization plus server-side validation.
[09:29] Sofia Ramos (Aurora): That's my preference — minimize token leakage. Also need confirmation that logs don't persist raw prompts in plain text.
[09:39] Maya Chen (Redwood): Understood — we'll send the logs retention and redaction policy.
[09:45] Rohit Patel (Redwood): Quick note on the 24h run I'm starting today — I plan to: ramp client weights, run two bucket thresholds (60% and 75%), and capture memory + hit rate + quality regression sample.
[10:00] David Kim (Aurora): When do you expect results?
[10:06] Rohit Patel (Redwood): 7 days for full signal but we should have a preliminary 24h report by Friday — so Oct 8th.
[10:14] Maya Chen (Redwood): Perfect. Any open concerns about private deployment readiness?
[10:21] Priya Shah (Aurora): We still need to confirm network egress controls and KMS HSM mapping.
[10:28] Sofia Ramos (Aurora): And audit logs retention period — will you support 7 years or is that unrealistic?
[10:36] Lena Ortiz (Redwood CSM): Seven years is probably an add-on enterprise compliance feature; we'll flag it to the legal/compliance team and get back.
[10:46] Marcus Lee (Aurora): One more thing — do you see degradation when KV hitrate is high but the model version changes? We want smooth rollouts.
[10:58] Rohit Patel (Redwood): We support canarying with independent KV namespaces per model version to avoid cross-version pollution, but that increases memory. You can use a fallthrough policy to read from previous namespace if needed.
[11:16] David Kim (Aurora): Nice. That solves migration pain.
[11:22] Maya Chen (Redwood): Ok wrapping up — recap next steps and owners. Rohit will run the 24h stress + compare 60/75 thresholds; David will export 1k prompts; Sofia will send security constraints; Maya will share Private deployment doc and audit notes.
[11:44] David Kim (Aurora): We'll also try the client-side canonicalizer patch on mobile v2 tomorrow.
[11:50] Maya Chen (Redwood): Great. We'll meet same time next week. Thanks everyone.
[12:00] Meeting end.
